characterList.description: An Italian astrophysicist and Research Director at INAF (Milan). She is the INAF representative in the CTA Consortium Board. She appears in a video call against a bookshelf backdrop, in a conference setting, and in an interview setting.

text_to_speech: I am an Italian astrophysicist. And I am the Director of Research at the National Institute of Astrophysics. In CTA, from the managerial point of view, I represent INAF within the Collaboration Board. From the scientific point of view, I have always been involved in high-energy astrophysics especially in gamma rays from space. Neutron stars are leftovers from supernova explosions. Remnants of the nucleus of very massive stars. Very magnetized, since the neutron star inherits the magnetic field of the primeval star. And also, very fast. Neutron stars are very, very fast rotators once again, since they inherit the rotational momentum the rotational energy of the primeval stars. The identification of Geminga has been a very long story.   It took 20 years to go from the first detection to the confirmation of the identification we had proposed. I remember very vividly a telephone call we got from the States from our Goddard colleagues saying that ROSAT had seen the pulsation of Geminga. It was 1992. And EGRET had confirmed it. We were very excited, of course. It was our source. We always had told colleagues that it was a pulsar not well behaved since it does not pulsate in radio wavelengths. But, it barks like a pulsar, it smells like a pulsar, it must be a pulsar. At this point we realized, right away, that we had the COS-B data. COS-B had looked to Geminga several times during its seven year-long lifetime. And so, maybe, in the COS-B data, the period was present. And sure enough, the period was there. And since we saw the period several times we were able to compute the period derivative and so, to compute the overall energetic of the source Plus, its distance confirming what we had suspected all the way that Geminga is a very nearby object. I have been very lucky in my career I had several exciting moments. The one I remember most vividly is when I opened an email from the editor of the Annual Review of Astronomy and Astrophysics. The email said: "Dear Dr. Caraveo, given your extensive experience on the high-energy emission from neutron stars we are pleased to invite you to write a review paper on the subject." It was very pleasing for me to say immediately yes. But then, I had to provide the manuscript for, I remember, it was September 2013. And I had to devote my summer, my summer vacation to write the paper. After a few evenings spent in such a way I remember my daughter telling me "But when will it be finished?" And I remember telling her, "I want it as much as you do!" But, eventually, I finished it. I am very often requested to give advice to girls at school and to young women at the university. "What is the most important quality that helps you making your way in the scientific career?" And my answer is always the same. You need to be determined. You need to be absolutely confident in your capabilities. It makes the difference. What is important in a career scientific or otherwise, in the world in general is the confidence you have in yourself and the determination you have to follow your dreams and to reach your goals.

youtube_description:
“You need to be determined, you need to be absolutely confident in your capabilities. What is important in a career is the determination you have to follow your dreams and to reach your goals.” These are the words that the renowned researcher and expert in high-energy emission from neutron stars, Prof. Patrizia Caraveo, dedicates to young female scientists and girls in STEM in the third episode of the “People of CTA” series. In this episode, Prof. Caraveo explains the history behind the identification of Geminga, the first radio-quiet pulsar ever detected, of which she was one of the principal investigators and one of the most exciting moments of her career.  

(full series: https://bit.ly/3pJv0EG)  #PeopleofCTA #astronomy #astrophysics #science
